lead: An endoscope lets a doctor look inside a body cavity through a natural opening or a small cut. It pipes light in along one bundle of glass fibres and brings the picture back along a second, ordered bundle, or along a tiny camera chip at the tip. Rigid tubes with glass rod lenses serve joints and the abdomen; flexible fibre-optic and video scopes reach the stomach and the colon. The same instrument carries a channel for forceps, suction and water, so the doctor can see, sample and treat in one pass.
prereq: You need Unit 1, Bioelectric Signals, Electrodes and Recorders, on physiological transducers, because the chip at a video scope's tip is a CCD or CMOS image sensor of that family.

sections.h3: The cavity problem and the rigid scope

blocks.text: An open cavity is dark and closed. To see inside without cutting it wide open, a doctor needs three things at once: light delivered into the cavity, an image carried back out, and a slim path for tools. An endoscope supplies all three. Every design, from a steel tube to a pill-sized camera, splits into the same parts: a lamp outside the body, an illumination path, an imaging path, a working channel, and controls at the handle.

The rigid endoscope is a straight metal tube, a few millimetres across, holding a relay of glass rod lenses. Each rod lens forms a real image of the previous one, so the picture is passed down the tube like a baton and arrives at an eyepiece or a camera head. Air gaps between the rods keep the lens power high, so the tube stays short. The optical result is a bright, sharp, wide view. The mechanical limit is the straight line: a rigid scope looks only where the tube already points.

Rigid scopes go where a straight path exists: through the abdominal wall (laparoscopy), into a knee or shoulder joint (arthroscopy), through the urethra into the bladder (cystoscopy). A few carry a prism at the tip to look 30° or 70° sideways while the tube itself stays straight.

sections.h3: How a flexible scope keeps the picture

blocks.text: Light travels along a glass fibre by total internal reflection. The fibre is a core of glass of refractive index n₁ wrapped in a cladding of slightly lower index n₂. A ray that strikes the core-cladding boundary steeper than the critical angle is reflected back inside and travels on.

blocks.where: θc is the critical angle, measured from the normal to the fibre wall; n₁ is the refractive index of the core; n₂ is the refractive index of the cladding, with n₂ < n₁. For n₁ = 1.50 and n₂ = 1.47, sin θc = 0.98 and θc ≈ 78°.

blocks.text: A flexible endoscope uses two separate bundles. The illumination bundle is incoherent: its fibres are packed at random and their only job is to pour light onto the tissue. The image bundle is coherent: fibre number 1 sits at the same corner of the bundle face at the handle as at the tip. Because the order never changes, a bright point at the tip leaves at one known point at the eyepiece, and a picture survives.

An objective lens at the tip focuses the tissue onto the face of the image bundle, and an eyepiece or camera magnifies what comes out. What the doctor sees is a mosaic of fibres. Two points closer together than one fibre width fall on the same fibre and merge, so many thin fibres give a finer picture but less light per fibre.
To aim the tip, two or four thin cables run down the shaft; a knob at the handle pulls one pair against the other and bends a springy section at the tip.

sections.h3: Video endoscopes, channels, cleaning and uses

blocks.text: The video endoscope removes the eyepiece. A CCD or CMOS sensor 1–2 mm across sits at the tip behind the objective lens, turns the image into an electrical signal, and wires carry it up the shaft to a processor and a monitor. The whole team watches one screen, and the image can be frozen, recorded and printed. A small light bundle usually remains, because the lamp and its heat stay outside the body.

A working channel runs the length of the shaft, typically 1.2 mm to 3.8 mm wide. Biopsy forceps, a snare or a laser fibre pass through it; the same channel gives suction, a water jet for washing, and air to inflate the cavity. Tip angulation and the channel together make the instrument a treatment tool, not just a camera.

The cleaning method is decided by what the instrument can survive. A rigid all-metal scope can be steam sterilised in an autoclave at 134 °C. A flexible scope cannot: heat and water ruin the fibre bundles, the seals and the sensor. It is leak-tested, cleaned, then disinfected chemically, for example in 2% glutaraldehyde for about 20 minutes, and hung to dry. A video scope's handle and connector are kept out of the liquid.

Capsule endoscopy is a swallowed pill holding a lens, a CMOS sensor, a battery and a radio. It sends images for about 8 hours and is passed out. It cannot be steered and takes no biopsy, so it is used where a flexible scope cannot reach.

examples.question: The image bundle of a flexible endoscope holds 10,000 fibres. Each fibre has a core diameter of 30 µm. (a) Find the light-carrying area of one fibre core. (b) Find the total core area of the bundle in mm². (c) Give one reason against simply using thicker fibres.
steps: Core radius r = d / 2 = 30 µm / 2 = 15 µm.
Area of one core A₁ = π r² = π × (15 µm)² = π × 225 µm² = 706.9 µm², that is about 707 µm².
Total core area A = N × A₁ = 10,000 × 706.9 µm² = 7.069 × 10⁶ µm².
Convert units: 1 mm² = 1000 µm × 1000 µm = 10⁶ µm², so A = 7.069 × 10⁶ / 10⁶ mm² = 7.07 mm².

Part (c): a thicker core carries more light per fibre, but each fibre then covers a larger spot on the image face. Two points closer than one core diameter (30 µm here) land on the same fibre and merge, so the picture becomes coarser.
examples.answer: One core carries about 707 µm² of light-carrying area, and the 10,000-fibre bundle gives a total core area of 7.07 mm²; thicker cores brighten the image but blur it.
examples.check:
import math
n = 10000
d_um = 30.0
r_um = d_um / 2.0
a_one = math.pi * r_um ** 2
total = n * a_one
print(round(a_one))
print(round(total / 1e6, 2))

traps: Swapping the two bundles: the incoherent bundle only carries light, the coherent bundle carries the image because its fibres keep the same order at both ends.
Placing the lamp at the tip. The lamp stays outside the body; in a video scope only the small sensor travels to the tip.
Treating a bigger fibre core as better resolution. A bigger core carries more light but resolves less, because resolution is set by the spacing of cores, core plus cladding.
Assuming every endoscope can be autoclaved. Steam at 134 °C destroys fibre bundles, seals and sensors, so flexible scopes are disinfected chemically instead.
Forgetting that a rigid scope sees only along a straight line, which is why it cannot do gastroscopy or colonoscopy.

quiz.q: Name the two fibre bundles in a flexible fibre-optic endoscope and state the job of each.
quiz.a: The illumination bundle, incoherent, carries light from the lamp to the tissue. The image bundle, coherent, carries the picture from the objective lens to the eyepiece.

quiz.q: Why must the image bundle be coherent while the light bundle need not be?
quiz.a: The light bundle only has to deliver energy, so the position of each fibre does not matter. The image bundle must map each point at the tip to one known point at the handle; if the fibres did not keep the same order at both ends, the picture would arrive scrambled.

quiz.q: A scope has 20,000 image fibres, each with core diameter 20 µm. Find the total core area in mm².
Why is a video scope's light bundle still needed when the image comes from a chip?
quiz.a: The chip senses light but makes none. The lamp and its heat stay outside the body, so a fibre bundle must bring the illumination to the tissue.

quiz.q: A flexible scope of the same outer diameter as a rigid scope gives a dimmer, coarser image. Explain both effects.
quiz.a: Only the fibre cores carry light; cladding and the gaps between packed fibres waste part of the face, so less light is collected than through a rod-lens relay. The picture is a mosaic of fibres, so detail finer than one core-plus-cladding spacing is lost.

quiz.q: Which scope type is chosen for a knee joint, and which for the stomach, and why?
quiz.a: A rigid arthroscope for the knee: the joint is reached through a short straight port and the rod-lens image is sharp. A flexible gastroscope for the stomach: the path through the mouth and oesophagus bends, so a rigid tube cannot follow it.

quiz.q: A designer widens the working channel of a flexible scope without changing its outer diameter. State the trade-off for the image.
quiz.a: The bundle must shrink to make room, so fewer or thinner fibres fit. Fewer fibres mean fewer picture elements; thinner fibres keep resolution but each carries less light, so the image is dimmer and the biopsy channel is bought at the cost of image quality.

beyond: Not for the exam. Capsule endoscopy is moving from a passive pill to a steerable one with a vibrating or magnetic drive. Single-use flexible scopes are sold to remove the disinfection step between patients, and their price is the deciding factor in Indian hospitals. Narrow-band and autofluorescence imaging add wavelength selection to the lamp so that early cancers stand out. Robotic and magnetic colonoscopes aim at the loop pain that makes the procedure hard. Search terms: capsule endoscope, disposable duodenoscope, narrow band imaging, magnetic capsule control.
